The `rubric` block (required components/connections, expected decision options, weights, canonical trade-offs) and per-item `explanation`/`feedback` are NEVER sent to the client before submission — see agent/sysdesign_bank.py public views. Decision prompts use stable option ids; grading compares the student's chosen set to the rubric's `expected`/`acceptable` set deterministically. `palette` lists allowed component ids; connections reference these ids. concept_ids map into agent/data/sysdesign_concepts.json.

scenarios.title: Design a URL Shortener
scenarios.prompt: Design a service like bit.ly that turns a long URL into a short code and redirects short codes back to the original URL. Optimize for very high read volume (redirects) relative to writes (new short links).
functional_requirements: Create a short code for a given long URL
Redirect a short code to its original URL

decision_prompts.prompt: Primary datastore for code -> URL mapping?

options.text: Relational (SQL) with an index on the short code
Key-value / NoSQL store keyed by short code
Flat files on disk
In-memory only, no persistence

decision_prompts.prompt: How to generate unique short codes?

options.text: Monotonic ID generator encoded in base62
Random code with collision check + retry
Let users type any code, first-come
Use the current timestamp as the code

decision_prompts.prompt: How to serve high read (redirect) volume? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Cache hot mappings in memory
Add read replicas of the datastore
Send all reads to one primary DB
Drop the index to speed up writes

decision_prompts.prompt: Which trade-offs apply to this design? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A KV store gives O(1) lookups but weaker ad-hoc querying
Caching adds a staleness/invalidation concern
This workload needs multi-row ACID transactions
Complex JOINs are central to the redirect path

feedback.components: A redirect service needs an app tier plus a cache for the hot short-code lookups.
feedback.connections: The app server should read through the cache before hitting the datastore.
feedback.data: Either a KV store keyed by code or a SQL table with an index on the code works; both give fast point lookups.
feedback.scalability: Cache hot mappings and add read replicas — reads dominate this workload.
feedback.tradeoffs: KV gives fast lookups at the cost of ad-hoc querying; caching introduces invalidation concerns.

scenarios.title: Design a News Feed
scenarios.prompt: Design a social news feed that shows each user a timeline of posts from accounts they follow. Handle users with very large follower counts and keep feed loads fast.
functional_requirements: A user can load a timeline of recent posts from followed accounts
nonfunctional_requirements: Handle celebrity accounts with millions of followers
Scale write and read paths independently

decision_prompts.prompt: How should the feed be assembled?

options.text: Fan-out on write (push to each follower's feed via workers)
Fan-out on read (pull + merge followed users' posts at read time)
Hybrid: fan-out on write, but pull for celebrity accounts
One global posts table scanned per request

decision_prompts.prompt: Where to store post media (images/video)?

options.text: Object storage fronted by a CDN
As BLOBs inside the primary database
On each app server's local disk
Only in the cache

decision_prompts.prompt: Which scaling techniques fit this system? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Load balance stateless app servers horizontally
Cache assembled feeds
Use a queue + workers for write fan-out
Vertically scale a single large server only

decision_prompts.prompt: Which trade-offs apply? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Fan-out on write amplifies writes for high-follower accounts
Fan-out on read shifts cost to read-time latency
Feeds can tolerate eventual consistency
Every follower must see new posts synchronously

feedback.components: A scalable feed needs async workers and a queue for fan-out plus a cache for assembled feeds.
feedback.connections: App servers enqueue fan-out work; workers consume the queue and write to per-user feed stores.
feedback.data: Store media in object storage behind a CDN, not in the primary DB.
feedback.scalability: Load-balance stateless app servers, cache feeds, and fan out via a queue + workers.
feedback.tradeoffs: Write fan-out amplifies writes for celebrities; read fan-out shifts cost to read time; feeds tolerate eventual consistency.

scenarios.title: Design a Rate Limiter
scenarios.prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter that caps how many requests a client (by API key) may make per time window, enforced consistently across many application servers.
functional_requirements: Allow or reject a request based on a per-client quota
Enforce the limit across all app servers
nonfunctional_requirements: Very low added latency per request
Fail gracefully if the limiter backend is briefly unavailable

decision_prompts.prompt: Where to keep the per-client counters?

options.text: A shared in-memory store (e.g. Redis) with atomic increments
Each app server's local memory
A SQL row updated per request
Append to a log file and count periodically

decision_prompts.prompt: Which rate-limiting algorithm?

options.text: Token bucket / sliding window
Randomly drop a fraction of requests
Block everything once any limit is near
No algorithm; rely on client honesty

decision_prompts.prompt: Where can the limiter be enforced? (Select all that apply)

options.text: At the API gateway / edge
As middleware in each app server
As a database trigger on every table
Only in the client, trusting it not to cheat

decision_prompts.prompt: Which trade-offs apply? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A shared counter adds a network hop but gives global accuracy
Local counters are fast but drift / over-admit across servers
You must decide fail-open vs fail-closed when the store is down
A per-request SQL update scales effortlessly to any load

feedback.components: Use an app tier plus a shared fast counter store for cross-server accuracy.
feedback.connections: Each app server (or the gateway) increments the shared counter atomically.
feedback.data: A shared in-memory store with atomic increments is the standard choice; local memory drifts.
feedback.scalability: Enforce at the gateway and/or app middleware; a token bucket / sliding window is typical.
feedback.tradeoffs: A shared counter trades a hop for accuracy; local counters over-admit; decide fail-open vs fail-closed.

scenarios.title: Design a Chat System
scenarios.prompt: Design a 1:1 and group messaging system that delivers messages in near-real-time, stores history, and works when recipients are offline.
functional_requirements: Send and receive messages in near-real-time
Deliver messages to offline users when they reconnect
nonfunctional_requirements: Low delivery latency for online users

decision_prompts.prompt: How should online clients receive messages?

options.text: Persistent connections (WebSocket) with a connection/presence layer
HTTP polling every second
Deliver each message by email
User manually refreshes the page

decision_prompts.prompt: Where to store message history?

options.text: A horizontally-partitioned store keyed by conversation
One unpartitioned SQL table for all messages forever
Only in the cache
Only on each client device

decision_prompts.prompt: How to handle offline delivery? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Queue undelivered messages for later
Send a push notification
Drop messages for offline users
Block the sender until the recipient is online

decision_prompts.prompt: Which trade-offs apply? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Persistent connections hold server state and need a presence/routing layer
Partitioning by conversation keeps per-conversation ordering simple
Frequent polling wastes resources and adds latency vs push
A single SQL table scales to unlimited message volume

feedback.components: Near-real-time chat needs a connection layer, a queue for offline delivery, and a partitioned history store.
feedback.connections: App servers publish to a queue; workers persist and push to offline recipients.
feedback.data: Partition message history by conversation; a single unpartitioned SQL table won't scale.
feedback.scalability: Queue undelivered messages and use push notifications for offline users.
feedback.tradeoffs: Persistent connections need presence/routing; conversation partitioning preserves ordering; polling is wasteful vs push.

scenarios.title: Design an Image Upload Service
scenarios.prompt: Design a service where users upload images, which are stored durably, processed into thumbnails, and served quickly worldwide.
functional_requirements: Serve images fast to a global audience
nonfunctional_requirements: Processing must not block the upload response

decision_prompts.prompt: Where to store the image files?

options.text: Object storage (durable, cheap, scalable)
As BLOBs in a relational database
On the app server's local disk
In the cache only

decision_prompts.prompt: How to generate thumbnails?

options.text: Enqueue a job; a worker processes it asynchronously
Resize inline during the upload request
Resize on every read request, every time
Have an admin resize images by hand

decision_prompts.prompt: How to serve images fast globally? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Serve via a CDN
Cache image metadata
Stream every image through the app servers each time
Disable all caching for freshness

decision_prompts.prompt: Which trade-offs apply? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Async processing makes uploads fast but thumbnails appear after a delay
Object storage scales far better than DB BLOBs for large files
A CDN improves latency but adds cost and cache-invalidation concerns
Local app-server disk is a durable, scalable choice

feedback.components: Store originals in object storage; process thumbnails with a queue + workers so uploads stay fast.
feedback.connections: The app writes the original to object storage and enqueues a processing job for a worker.
feedback.data: Object storage is the right home for large files, not DB BLOBs or local disk.
feedback.scalability: Serve through a CDN and cache metadata; don't stream every image through the app tier.
feedback.tradeoffs: Async processing delays thumbnails; object storage beats BLOBs; a CDN adds cost and invalidation concerns.
